		if(url == null){
		  url = window.location.href;
		}

	    if (!results) return null;
	    if (!results[2]) return '';
	    return decodeURIComponent(results[2].replace(/\+/g, ' '));
	}

    ;(function(win, doc, style, timeout) {
    var STYLE_ID = 'at-body-style';
    function getParent() {
    return doc.getElementsByTagName('head')[0];
    }
    function addStyle(parent, id, def) {
        if (!parent) {
        return;
        }
        var style = doc.createElement('style');
        style.id = id;
        style.innerHTML = def;
        parent.appendChild(style);
    }
    function removeStyle(parent, id) {
        if (!parent) {
            return;
        }
        var style = doc.getElementById(id);
        if (!style) {
            return;
        }
        parent.removeChild(style);
    }
    addStyle(getParent(), STYLE_ID, style);
    setTimeout(function() {
    removeStyle(getParent(), STYLE_ID);
    }, timeout);

    /**
 * String.prototype.replaceAll() polyfill
 * https://gomakethings.com/how-to-replace-a-section-of-a-string-with-another-one-with-vanilla-js/
 * @author Chris Ferdinandi
 * @license MIT
 */
if (!String.prototype.replaceAll) {
	String.prototype.replaceAll = function(str, newStr){
		// If a regex pattern
		if (Object.prototype.toString.call(str).toLowerCase() === '[object regexp]') {
			return this.replace(str, newStr);
		}
		// If a string
		return this.replace(new RegExp(str, 'g'), newStr);
	};

	function getCookie(cname) {
	 	var name = cname + "=";
  		var decodedCookie = decodeURIComponent(document.cookie);
		var ca = decodedCookie.split(';');
  		for(var i = 0; i <ca.length; i++) {
    			var c = ca[i];
    			while (c.charAt(0) == ' ') {
     				 c = c.substring(1);
    			}
    			if (c.indexOf(name) == 0) {
    				 return c.substring(name.length, c.length);
    			}
  		}
  		return "";
	}

function addStyle(styles) {            
    /* Create style document */
    var css = document.createElement('style');
    css.type = 'text/css';

    if (css.styleSheet) 
        css.styleSheet.cssText = styles;
    else 
        css.appendChild(document.createTextNode(styles));

    /* Append style to the tag name */
    document.getElementsByTagName("head")[0].appendChild(css);
}
function httpGet(theUrl,req_type) {
    if (window.XMLHttpRequest) { // code for IE7+, Firefox, Chrome, Opera, Safari
        xmlhttp=new XMLHttpRequest();
    } else {// code for IE6, IE5
        xmlhttp=new ActiveXObject("Microsoft.XMLHTTP");
    }
    xmlhttp.onreadystatechange=function()
    {
        if (xmlhttp.readyState==4 && xmlhttp.status==200)
        {
            if(req_type == 'menu_html'){
            var nav_text = xmlhttp.responseText.replaceAll('https://static.cloud.coveo.com/searchui/v2.9159/js/CoveoJsSearch.Lazy.min.js', '');
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll('src="/', 'src="'+maindomain_lang+'/');
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll("src='/", "src='"+maindomain_lang+"/");
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll("'/content", "'"+maindomain_lang+"/content");
                        
            document.getElementById("PAN_2021_NAV_ASYNC").innerHTML = nav_text.replaceAll('href="/', 'href="'+maindomain_lang+'/');

            var lozad_back = document.getElementsByClassName('lozad-background');
            Array.prototype.forEach.call(lozad_back, function(el) {
            // Do stuff here
            var el_back_img_path = el.getAttribute('data-background-image');
            var first_pos = el_back_img_path.indexOf("'");
            var last_pos = el_back_img_path.indexOf("'",first_pos+1);
            el_back_img_path = el_back_img_path.substring(first_pos+1,last_pos);
            let result = el_back_img_path.includes(main_site_url);
            if(result == false){
                el.setAttribute("data-background-image",main_site_url+el_back_img_path);
            }
            else{
                el.setAttribute("data-background-image",el_back_img_path);
            }
            });
            const observer_lozad = lozad('.lozad, .lozad-background'); // lazy loads elements with default selector as '.lozad'
            observer_lozad.observe();
            }
            if(req_type == 'head_inline_css'){
            addStyle(xmlhttp.responseText);
            }
        }
    }
    xmlhttp.open("GET", theUrl, true );
    xmlhttp.send();    
}

                <h2><a id="post-187630-_4lt92rr5muov"></a>Executive Summary</h2>
<p>We discovered that an Iranian state-aligned threat actor has been masquerading as the Dubai Airports IT department to deliver trojanized coding challenges to high-value targets. Unit 42 tracks the activity as CL-STA-1178. This activity includes a campaign we call “Blinder Tunnel,” that targeted Iraqi critical infrastructure in March 2026, following infrastructure staging that was observed as early as November 2025. We named the campaign Blinder Tunnel after infrastructure terms the attackers used, as well as the malware’s tunneling capabilities.</p>
<p>While other security vendors have discussed individual attacks linked to this activity, this is the first report that not only ties together these disparate attacks as related activity, but tracks the evolving 2026 activity and the Blinder Tunnel campaign as a whole. We assess with high confidence that this activity aligns with an Iranian-nexus threat.</p>
<p>This campaign expands on previous operations and incorporates a “Peaky Blinders” theme by naming infrastructure components after the British crime drama’s branding — even embedding its theme song into the malware.</p>
<p>During our research, we discovered that the attackers established an initial foothold using a three-step attack chain:</p>
<ol>
<li>Exploited legitimate Windows developer <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.csproj</span> files</li>
<li>Performed <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">AppDomainManager</span> hijacking</li>
<li>Executed binaries through DLL sideloading</li>
</ol>
<p>These steps enabled the attackers to deploy custom malware that we refer to as ShelbyLoader V2. To blend in with legitimate cloud traffic, the campaign misused GitHub’s API infrastructure for command-and-control (C2) communication. It did so by leveraging repositories to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Fetch decryption keys</li>
<li>Download payloads</li>
<li>Use GitHub issues as a resilient C2 fallback mechanism</li>
</ul>
<p>GitHub has taken down the malicious infrastructure that we identified as being associated with this campaign.</p>
<p>Our investigation benefited from various operational security (OpSec) and cryptographic missteps by the attackers, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>Exposing tools on public repositories</li>
<li>Combining phishing and tunneling infrastructure</li>
<li>Embedding metadata within the show’s theme song</li>
</ul>
<p>These tactical errors linked Blinder Tunnel infrastructure to a separate campaign in which the same actor leveraged conflict-themed Google Drive lures for credential harvesting against an Israeli entity in May-June 2026.</p>
<p>Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the Blinder Tunnel campaign through the following products and services:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/wildfire" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced WildFire</a></li>
<li><a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/advanced-url-filtering" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced URL Filtering</a> and <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/dns-security" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced DNS Security</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cortex/cortex-xdr?_gl=1*13pmp8e*_ga*NzQyNjM2NzkuMTY2NjY3OTczNw..*_ga_KS2MELEEFC*MTY2OTczNjA2MS4zMS4wLjE2Njk3MzYwNjEuNjAuMC4w" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cortex XDR</a> and <a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/resources/datasheets/cortex-xsiam-aag" target="_blank" rel="noopener">XSIAM</a></li>
</ul>
<p>Cortex <a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/r/Cortex-AgentiX/Cortex-AgentiX-Documentation/Get-Started-with-Cortex-AgentiX" target="_blank" rel="noopener">AgentiX</a> Agentic Assistant streamlined this investigation.</p>
<p>If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the <a href="https://start.paloaltonetworks.com/contact-unit42.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Unit 42 Incident Response team</a>.</p>
<table style="width: 100%;">

<h2><a id="post-187630-_j6gqwnduwpf"></a>Introduction</h2>
<p>CL-STA-1178 represents activity from an Iranian state-aligned threat actor linked to a series of targeted cyber operations across the Middle East. Previously associated with campaigns tracked by Elastic Security Labs as <a href="https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/the-shelby-strategy" target="_blank" rel="noopener">The Shelby Strategy</a>, the threat actor behind this cluster of activity frequently employs thematic branding in their malware and infrastructure, drawing inspiration from the popular television show “Peaky Blinders.”</p>
<p>The attackers behind this cluster target high-value infrastructure, including telecommunications, aviation and other critical entities across Iraq, Israel and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).</p>
<p>Since the launch of Blinder Tunnel in March 2026, Unit 42 researchers have identified an evolution in the operational capabilities associated with the activity. The attackers used tailored social engineering tactics, weaponizing recruitment lures aimed at Iraqi software developers and engineers.</p>
<p>We observed the threat actor staging and testing attack infrastructure as early as November 2025. This infrastructure remained dormant but operational until March 2026, when the attackers activated the campaign to target an individual in Iraq's critical infrastructure sector.</p>
<p>The infection chain relies on three initial execution techniques to establish covert access. The attacks introduced a new layer of evasion by weaponizing a native <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.csproj</span> file, a Microsoft developer file used to build software projects. This initial stage subsequently triggered <a href="https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/014/" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">AppDomainManager</span> hijacking</a>, followed by <a href="https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/001/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">DLL sideloading</a>, leveraging their previously established execution techniques.</p>
<p><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">AppDomainManager</span> hijacking is an emerging evasion technique that attackers are increasingly adopting, according to our recent research. Iranian threat groups like <a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tracking-iran-apt-screening-serpens/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Screening Serpens</a> and others are using this technique to force trusted Windows applications to covertly execute malicious payloads.</p>
<p>For C2 communication, the attackers behind Blinder Tunnel misuses legitimate GitHub API infrastructure, a strategy known as living off the cloud, to blend their malicious network activity with standard enterprise traffic. Before its removal, the GitHub repository also hosted an in-memory wrapper that executed the open-source <a href="https://github.com/jpillora/chisel" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Chisel</a> tunneling utility. The attackers used Chisel as a bridge between their external infrastructure and compromised networks.</p>
<p>Figure 1 provides a high-level view of the entire campaign.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187631" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187631" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187631 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-452541-187630-1.png" alt="Diagram illustrating the Blinder Tunnel campaign. The process begins with an access vector impersonating airport Wi‑Fi, leading to a three‑step execution chain involving malicious AppDomainManager and DLL sideloading. Core functions utilize ShelbyLoader V2, with components like ShelbyC2 V2 and PowerShell commands. Parallel phishing targets are shown using the same IPs. " width="1000" height="706" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-452541-187630-1.png 2002w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-452541-187630-1-623x440.png 623w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-452541-187630-1-991x700.png 991w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-452541-187630-1-768x542.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-452541-187630-1-1536x1085.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187631" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 1. Overview of the Blinder Tunnel campaign.</figcaption></figure>
<h2><a id="post-187630-_j6gqwnduwpf"></a>Initial Access and Delivery</h2>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_ea108tj79l1o"></a>Dubai Airports Careers Portal</h3>
<p>Starting in late March 2026, the threat actor launched a social engineering campaign disguised as a professional recruitment process to compromise a specific individual, likely a software engineer. We identified this campaign through VirusTotal, following multiple file submissions from a submitter based in Iraq.</p>
<p>Impersonating the Dubai Airports IT department, the attackers approached a target with a job offer for a development role. Threat actors often abuse, take advantage of or subvert legitimate products for malicious purposes. This does not imply that the legitimate product is flawed or malicious. Unit 42 is not aware of any breach, compromise, or vulnerability within Dubai Airports infrastructure or systems.</p>
<p>As a mandatory first stage in the recruitment process, attackers instructed the target to download and install a file named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Dubai Airport Careers</span>.</p>
<p>This file was an Inno Setup installer that deployed a self-contained, offline site masquerading as a career portal. To access the assessment, the target had to log in using credentials provided by the “recruiters,” simulating a realistic portal experience.</p>
<p>Figure 2 shows the initial login screen.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187642" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187642" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187642 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-456111-187630-2.png" alt="Screenshot of a login screen for &quot;Dubai Airports Careers&quot; featuring input fields for username and password, and a login button. The logo and text are on the right, with a profile icon in a circle on the left." width="1000" height="483" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-456111-187630-2.png 1980w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-456111-187630-2-786x380.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-456111-187630-2-1450x700.png 1450w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-456111-187630-2-768x371.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-456111-187630-2-1536x742.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187642" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 2. Impersonated Dubai Airports career portal login page.</figcaption></figure>
<p>After the target logged in, the application presented a tailored, 10-question HR questionnaire. Figure 2 shows part of this questionnaire.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187653" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187653" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187653 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-459436-187630-3.png" alt="Screenshot of a form titled &quot;Dubai Airports Careers Q&amp;A&quot; with four questions for applicants to answer. The questions focus on personal attraction to the position, relevant experience, strengths, and handling tight deadlines or pressure. The form header includes the Dubai Airports logo and its name written in both English and Arabic." width="1000" height="997" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-459436-187630-3.png 1310w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-459436-187630-3-441x440.png 441w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-459436-187630-3-702x700.png 702w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-459436-187630-3-300x300.png 300w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-459436-187630-3-768x766.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187653" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 3. Impersonated question and answer page mimicking an application for potential job candidates.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Submitting the questionnaire does not trigger data exfiltration, remote communication or malicious execution. This lack of network or backend activity indicates that the application is a harmless decoy. This lack of suspicious activity is designed to build credibility and lower the victim's guard before delivering a malicious payload in the next phase of the phishing operation.</p>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_jplkikwqg2jd"></a>Recruitment Coding Challenge</h3>
<p>In April 2026, the same source that reported the career portal to VirusTotal made another submission, revealing the next stage of the recruitment lure. Unlike the usual malicious links or documents seen in <a href="https://www.clearskysec.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Iranian-Dream-Job-ver1.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">a report by ClearSky Cyber Security about Iranian Dream Job</a> campaigns, the threat actor sent the target a weaponized Microsoft Visual Studio project archive disguised as a coding assessment.</p>
<p>The project, named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">DubaiAirport_Carrers_IT_Test.zip</span> (misspelled <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Carrers</span> instead of <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Careers</span>), contained a Readme.md file with personalized instructions. The message addressed the target directly:</p>
<ul>
<li>“Dear <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">&lt;redacted full name&gt;</span>.”</li>
</ul>
<p>The sender claimed to be a senior manager of a Dubai Airports IT department, instructing the recipient to open the C# <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Flight Management System</span> project in their integrated development environment (IDE).</p>
<p>Figure 4 shows the first section of the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Readme.md</span> file, including the message tailored to the target and instructions for an at-home assessment.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187664" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187664" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187664 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-463021-187630-4.png" alt="Screenshot of a scam email claiming interest from Dubai Airport IT Department. The email mentions assessing problem-solving and debugging skills with a coding challenge using Visual Studio or any preferred C# IDE, suggesting a home task estimated to take 15-20 minutes." width="1000" height="221" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-463021-187630-4.png 1776w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-463021-187630-4-786x173.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-463021-187630-4-768x170.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-463021-187630-4-1536x339.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187664" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 4. The opening section of the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Readme.md</span> file.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Under the pretense of evaluating the target's technical abilities, the project included an intentional bug in a backend C# method: a <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">for</span> loop that skips the last element. Attackers instructed the target to build and run the project to find and fix the bug, a task that an experienced software engineer could accomplish without difficulty.</p>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_rse6fv4pis0n"></a>Three-Step Infection Chain</h3>
<p>The initial infection is triggered by a malicious <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.csproj</span> file. Once executed, the attack chain progressed to <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">AppDomainManager</span> hijacking followed by DLL sideloading.</p>
<h4><a id="post-187630-_pbqt8goo5z7z"></a>Stage One: Malicious .csproj File</h4>
<p>The attackers weaponized the C# project's <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.csproj</span> configuration file by misusing <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/msbuild/build-process-overview?view=visualstudio" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Visual Studio's built-in evaluation process</a>. This method caused the payload to execute the moment the project was loaded into the IDE, even before the developer attempted to compile the code.</p>
<p>Figure 5 shows the project files within the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">DubaiAirport_Carrers_IT_Test.zip</span> archive, including the weaponized <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.csproj</span> file.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187675" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187675" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187675 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-465543-187630-5.png" alt="Screenshot of a file directory showing several folders and files. Notable entries include a highlighted &quot;Resources&quot; folder, described as containing a malicious payload." width="1000" height="520" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-465543-187630-5.png 1570w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-465543-187630-5-786x409.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-465543-187630-5-1347x700.png 1347w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-465543-187630-5-768x399.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-465543-187630-5-1536x798.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187675" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 5. The project's structure and files within the malicious archive.</figcaption></figure>
<p>When a developer opens a project, Visual Studio performs a design-time build in the background. This process resolves dependencies and enables various features. During this initialization phase, Visual Studio runs a specific command called <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">GetFrameworkPaths</span>. Building on this command, the attackers defined a custom XML target with this exact name in their malicious <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.csproj</span> file, overriding the safe Microsoft default behavior.</p>
<p>When the target opened the project, Visual Studio attempted its routine background check and executed the attacker's custom instructions without user intervention. The script created a deceptive folder in the user's local app data: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\RuntimeBrokers</span>. It then copied the hidden malware binaries from the project's <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Resources</span> folder to this directory and launched the payload, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBroker.exe</span>.</p>
<p>Figure 6 demonstrates the exact configuration of the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.csproj</span> file, highlighting the hijacked target and the sequence that copied the malicious files to their target destination.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187686" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187686" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187686 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-468739-187630-6.png" alt="Screenshot of code related to potential malware activities. It shows an XML configuration with highlighted sections indicating actions. Key actions include creating a directory for Microsoft RuntimeBrokers, copying files from Resources to this new directory, and executing a payload." width="1000" height="456" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-468739-187630-6.png 1720w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-468739-187630-6-786x358.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-468739-187630-6-1536x700.png 1536w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-468739-187630-6-768x350.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187686" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 6. The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.csproj</span> file configuration, showing the malicious configuration used by the threat actor.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The malware deployed, copied itself and launched in the background while the developer was still reading the deceptive <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Readme.md</span> file. This technique is classified as <a href="https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1127/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution</a>. It can be effective because the malicious background execution is triggered by the legitimate, expected behavior of <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">msbuild.exe</span>, a trusted developer tool.</p>
<h4><a id="post-187630-_7xegw4tszsmp"></a>Stage Two: AppDomainManager Hijacking</h4>
<p>The MSBuild binary launched a legitimate, signed Microsoft Visual Studio hosting process (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">vshost.exe</span>). This file was then renamed to <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBroker.exe</span>. Upon execution, the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">AppDomainManager</span> hijacking began by manipulating the application's <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBroker.exe.config</span> file. The attackers used this configuration file to replace the application's default startup manager with their own malicious version. This forced the system to pass full execution control to the malware before the host application launched, allowing their custom RAT, ShelbyLoader V2, to run in a hidden, trusted process.</p>
<p>Using this hijack technique allowed the attackers to manipulate the system and security configurations. By adding just a few lines of XML, the attacker instructed the system to disable one of its security-tracking mechanisms using the &lt;<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">etwEnable enabled=</span>"<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">false</span>"<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">/</span>&gt; directive.</p>
<p>Because Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) is critical for monitoring execution and detecting in-memory threats, this flag could impair detection capabilities.</p>
<p>Figure 7 shows the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBroker.exe.config</span> configuration file content, with the embedded malicious lines.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187697" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187697" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187697 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-471486-187630-7.png" alt="Screenshot of a code snippet from a configuration file. Highlighted items include &quot;etwEnable&quot; set to &quot;true&quot; and &quot;false,&quot; and &quot;appDomainManagerType&quot;." width="1000" height="195" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-471486-187630-7.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-471486-187630-7-786x153.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-471486-187630-7-1920x374.png 1920w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-471486-187630-7-768x150.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-471486-187630-7-1536x299.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187697" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 7. <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBroker.exe.config</span> content.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Figure 8 displays the malicious files from the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Resources</span> folder, which served as the actor's main tool set throughout this campaign.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187708" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187708" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187708 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-474308-187630-8.png" alt="Screenshot of a file directory showing a list of files with types, sizes, and comments. Each file is labeled with comments in red dashed boxes, indicating their functions or connections to ShelbyLoader V2 and ShelbyC2 V2." width="1000" height="424" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-474308-187630-8.png 1692w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-474308-187630-8-786x334.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-474308-187630-8-1650x700.png 1650w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-474308-187630-8-768x326.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-474308-187630-8-1536x652.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187708" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 8. List of malicious files from the project's Resources folder.</figcaption></figure>
<h4><a id="post-187630-_i5zfab2zat4s"></a>Stage Three: DLL Sideloading</h4>
<p>Following the execution of <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBroker.exe</span> and the subsequent AppDomainManager hijack, the attack sequence concluded with DLL sideloading as its final stage.</p>
<p><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBroker.exe</span>, a renamed benign Microsoft binary, is susceptible to DLL search-order hijacking. The actor exploited this flaw to perform DLL sideloading, executing the malicious payload by loading <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBroker.dll</span> into memory.</p>
<p>Organizations can defend against these attacks by monitoring binaries that load unknown or non-standard DLLs outside of system directories. In this particular case, Cortex XDR flagged the root <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.slnx</span> file that triggered the DLL sideloading attempt as a high-severity threat, preventing execution before any user interaction could occur, as Figure 9 shows.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187719" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187719" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187719 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-477097-187630-9.png" alt="Screenshot of Cortex XDR interface related to DLL hijacking. It shows that an incident is flagged as high severity and highlights a DLL sideload attempt. It mentions detection by XDR and notes the file name as the root cause of the malicious activity. Various sections detail the attack tactics and evidence, including process execution and file path information." width="1000" height="977" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-477097-187630-9.png 1210w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-477097-187630-9-450x440.png 450w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-477097-187630-9-717x700.png 717w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-477097-187630-9-768x750.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187719" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 9. The infection chain originating in malicious DLL sideloading (categorized as DLL Hijacking), as shown, detected and prevented by Cortex XDR.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Security teams can detect this masquerading activity by monitoring abnormal process behavior. Cortex XDR flagged this execution chain as high risk and blocked the threat, as Figure 10 shows.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187730" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187730" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187730 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-479703-187630-10.png" alt="Screenshot of a Cortex XDR report indicating a high severity incident involving WildFire malware detection and masquerading activity on RuntimeBroker.exe. The report shows a sequence of five processes . A note indicates that the file initiates a DLL sideloading sequence to load the attacker's payload." width="1000" height="495" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-479703-187630-10.png 1762w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-479703-187630-10-786x389.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-479703-187630-10-1414x700.png 1414w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-479703-187630-10-768x380.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-479703-187630-10-1536x760.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187730" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 10. The infection chain as seen, detected and prevented by Cortex XDR.</figcaption></figure>
<h2><a id="post-187630-_jfd5huloejov"></a>The Attackers’ Evolving Tool Set</h2>
<p>The attacker’s tool set relied on a modular, multi-stage architecture. This architecture was designed for persistence, remote command execution and lateral movement across compromised environments. The following analysis examines the core components of the attacker’s custom tool set:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>ShelbyLoader V2</strong>: Primary loader that uses GitHub issues as a C2 fallback</li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;"><strong>PsProxy.dll</strong>:</span> PowerShell execution engine</li>
<li><strong>ShelbyC2 V2</strong>: Primary backdoor</li>
<li><strong>Blackwood</strong>: Loader running in-memory tunneling utility (Chisel)</li>
</ul>
<p>All the .NET binaries recovered in this campaign were obscured with the open-source obfuscator <a href="https://github.com/obfuscar/obfuscar" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Obfuscar</a>. This tool hinders reverse engineering and automated static analysis, using runtime string decryption and non-printable Unicode characters for class and method identifiers.</p>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_92t1u8j0zntp"></a>ShelbyLoader V2 RuntimeBroker.dll Loader</h3>
<p><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBroker.dll</span>, which we named ShelbyLoader V2, is a newer version of the <a href="https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/the-shelby-strategy" target="_blank" rel="noopener">previously documented ShelbyLoader malware</a>.</p>
<p>The malware was a C# DLL that performed the following activities:</p>
<ul>
<li>Operated as a loader</li>
<li>Created persistence</li>
<li>Fingerprinted the infected host</li>
<li>Established communication with the C2</li>
</ul>
<p>The malware served as the initial entry point for launching the campaign. It executed a structured routine to perform initial host anti-analysis checks and establish communication before downloading and decrypting a second-stage payload.</p>
<p>The malware utilized two timed mechanisms to manage its operations:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Persistence (120-second interval):</strong> The malware achieved persistence through the registry, by creating a <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">MicrosoftRuntime</span> value under the current user startup registry key, pointing to the binary located at <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\RuntimeBrokers\RuntimeBroker.exe</span>. The loader logged this persistence status across four operational states and returned the results to the attackers' C2:
<ul>
<li>Already persisted</li>
<li>Newly persisted</li>
<li>Registry key not found</li>
<li>Executable not found</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>Beacon (63-second interval):</strong> This timer drove the primary C2 loop. The beacon routine attempted to authenticate to the GitHub API using a hard-coded GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT): <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">github_pat_11B2HDA2Q0KDdo…(redacted)</span></li>
</ul>
<p>The beacon cycle began by communicating with the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">peakyblinders-tm/myLic</span> GitHub repository and uploading a Base64-encoded machine fingerprint to <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">/{machineId}/Lic.txt</span>. The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">machineId</span> is derived by taking the first 16 lowercase hex characters of a SHA-256 hash of the string <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Peaky Blinders 2.1</span> concatenated with the machine fingerprint.</p>
<p>After successful registration, the malware continuously polled for tasking by downloading the content of <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">/{machineId}/Inf.txt</span>. The malware parsed the response for a Base64-encoded command, which it decoded and executed. Once processed, the beacon uploaded an acknowledgment containing the SHA-256 file to update and clear the repository file. If the GitHub API returned an <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">HTTP 403 (Forbidden)</span> error due to rate limits, the malware enforced a one-hour sleep loop.</p>
<p>To hinder analysis, the malware checked for virtualization markers in the following locations:</p>
<ul>
<li>Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI)</li>
<li>Running processes</li>
<li>Registry keys</li>
<li>File artifacts</li>
</ul>
<p>It also verified host hardware (CPU, RAM, disk space) and ensured it was spawned by <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">explorer.exe</span> before running.</p>
<h4><a id="post-187630-_5whxtojvh66h"></a>GitHub Issues as a C2 Fallback Mechanism</h4>
<p>If the hard-coded token was revoked or the primary C2 channel returned an <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">HTTP 401 Unauthorized</span> error, the malware activated a fallback mechanism: a dead-drop resolver that leveraged the <a href="https://api.github.com/search/issues" target="_blank" rel="noopener">GitHub Issues Search API</a>.</p>
<p>The malware constructed an automated search query using the current date formatted as <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">yyyymmdd</span>, combined with the repository identifier and an issue type filter. For every matching issue found, it fetched the comments URL and parsed the response body. It then extracted specific content that was hidden inside standard HTML comment markers: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">&lt;!-- and --&gt;</span>.</p>
<p>This extracted ciphertext was decrypted using AES-256-CBC. The decryption key was derived by running an MD5 hash of the current date string, concatenated with the unique <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">machineId</span> and an initialization vector (IV) derived from the MD5 of that key, iterated five times. Once decrypted, the malware applied regular expressions to update the C2 owner, repository path and authentication token:</p>
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Owner=(\w.+)</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">LicRepo=(\w.+)</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">LicToken=(\w.+)</span></li>
</ul>
<p>This fallback structure was built to allow for continuous operations in the event that GitHub took down the primary C2 repository or security tools blocked it.</p>
<p>The operators also planted encrypted fallback C2 data within the comments of benign GitHub issues. The underlying text cannot be decrypted without a target's unique <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">machineId</span>. However, the campaign's overall timeline suggests that an issue comment posted on April 16, 2026, served as a potential additional C2 of this implant, as Figure 11 shows.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187741" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187741" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187741 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-482661-187630-11.png" alt="Screenshot of a code editor with text. A comment by &quot;peakyblinders-tm&quot; on April 16, 2026, includes highlighted sections: a regular expression for locating a specific comment, and an encrypted block labeled as containing a backup." width="1000" height="591" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-482661-187630-11.png 1490w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-482661-187630-11-745x440.png 745w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-482661-187630-11-1185x700.png 1185w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-482661-187630-11-768x454.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187741" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 11. A comment left by the attacker on April 16, 2026.</figcaption></figure>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_ty0962t9wudf"></a>PsProxy.dll: The PowerShell Proxy Module</h3>
<p>To execute local commands, the attackers used a dedicated in-memory module, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">PsProxy.dll</span>, which served as a stateless execution engine with no standalone network or persistence capabilities.</p>
<p>The malware leveraged a technique described by <a href="https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/#:~:text=PowerShell%20commands%2Fscripts%20can%20also,Common%20Language%20Interface%20(CLI)." target="_blank" rel="noopener">MITRE</a> as executing PowerShell commands without invoking the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">PowerShell.exe</span> binary. Security tools generally hunt for malicious activity by monitoring the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">PowerShell.exe</span> process. To evade this detection, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">PsProxy.dll</span> bypassed the standard console and hooked into the core PowerShell engine (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">System.Management.Automation.dll</span>).</p>
<p>The malware then initialized a customized <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/et-ee/powershell/scripting/developer/hosting/creating-runspaces?view=powershell-7.7" target="_blank" rel="noopener">runspace</a> — an invisible, self-contained execution context — within the hijacked host process. This allowed the attacker's script to execute without spawning <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">PowerShell.exe</span>.</p>
<p>The malware authors designed this architecture for both stealth and stability. The PowerShell module ran without dropping malicious scripts to the disk or spawning suspicious processes. It also operated in a separate memory compartment, preventing a crashed script from disrupting the primary C2 connection. When a command arrived from the server, the main payload passed the raw script over to this proxy for execution.</p>
<p>Figure 12 illustrates the role of <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">PsProxy.dll</span> within the attack chain as a secondary execution module for the ShelbyC2 V2 RAT.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187752" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187752" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187752 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-485816-187630-12.png" alt="Diagram illustrating the execution chain of ShelbyC2 V2 and PsProxy.dll. It shows the flow from ShelbyC2 V2 C2 sending a malicious script to PsProxy.dll, which acts as an in-memory module. The process then hijacks PowerShell.exe, showing the PsProxy.dll as a core component within a custom runspace, executing scripts and providing command output. Arrows indicate the direction of data flow." width="1000" height="1253" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-485816-187630-12.png 1026w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-485816-187630-12-351x440.png 351w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-485816-187630-12-558x700.png 558w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-485816-187630-12-768x963.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187752" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 12. PowerShell module functionality.</figcaption></figure>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_1fsgg1czv02i"></a>ShelbyC2 V2 RuntimeBrokerApi.dll: Loading the Final Payload</h3>
<p>Once the malware established stable communication with the GitHub-hosted C2, the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBroker.dll</span> loader read an AES-CBC-encrypted file named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBrokerApi.dll</span> from its base directory. We named this main RAT ShelbyC2 V2, based on the name of its last reported iteration, <a href="https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/the-shelby-strategy#:~:text=SHELBYC2%20code%20analysis" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ShelbyC2</a>.</p>
<p>The decryption key was generated using the full SHA-256 hash of a license content string fetched at runtime from the GitHub C2:</p>
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">hxxps[:]//api.github[.]com/repos/peakyblinders-tm/myLic/contents/{machineId}/Lic.txt</span></li>
</ul>
<p>The IV was set to the first 16 bytes of that same hash. The decrypted bytes were then loaded into memory as a raw .NET assembly.</p>
<p>ShelbyC2 V2 (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBrokerApi.dll</span>) operated as the primary RAT. It managed command execution via the previously analyzed <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">PsProxy.dll</span> PowerShell module and served as the staging mechanism for deploying the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Blackwood</span> tunneling tool into the network, which we analyze in detail in the following section.</p>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_j6gqwnduwpf"></a>Blackwood: A Custom, Zero-Disk Chisel Tunneling Tool</h3>
<p>On May 1, 2026, the attackers expanded their GitHub-centric infrastructure by creating a new public repository named pubs under the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">peakyblinders-tm</span> account. This repository hosted a single archive file: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Client.zip</span>. Our analysis of this payload revealed a malicious executable internally named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Blackwood</span>, which was previously covered by <a href="https://www.cpx.net/insights/blogs/uncovering-the-chinese-apt-group-net-malware-payload-part-1/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">CPX</a> and submitted to VirusTotal in May 2025.</p>
<p>Figure 13 shows the GitHub repository <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">pubs</span>, containing the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Client.zip</span> file.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187763" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187763" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187763 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-488182-187630-13.png" alt="Screenshot of a GitHub repository page for &quot;peakyblinders-tm/pubs&quot;. The repository has one branch and no tags, with the latest commit labeled &quot;Add files via upload&quot;." width="1000" height="506" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-488182-187630-13.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-488182-187630-13-786x398.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-488182-187630-13-1382x700.png 1382w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-488182-187630-13-768x389.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-488182-187630-13-1536x778.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187763" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 13. GitHub <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">pubs</span> repository containing the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Client.zip</span> file.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Figure 14 shows the extracted archive content, where the malicious file is named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Blackwood.dll</span>.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187774" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187774" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187774 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-491128-187630-14.png" alt="Screenshot of a File Explorer window displaying a folder named &quot;Client&quot; with several files. The files vary in type and size, with modification dates listed." width="1000" height="379" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-491128-187630-14.png 1388w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-491128-187630-14-786x298.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-491128-187630-14-768x291.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187774" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 14. Extracted <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Client.zip</span> archive content.</figcaption></figure>
<p>To deploy <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Blackwood</span>, the attackers relied on the same execution playbook observed with the primary loader, ShelbyLoader V2: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">AppDomainManager</span> hijacking and DLL sideloading. Inside the extracted archive, the attackers stored:</p>
<ul>
<li>The malicious payload</li>
<li>A legitimate Microsoft-signed binary, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">vshost32.exe</span></li>
<li>A configuration file named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">vshost32.exe.config</span></li>
</ul>
<p>When the trusted <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">vshost32.exe</span> executable was launched, the .NET runtime parsed the configuration file and sideloaded <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Blackwood.dll</span> into the application's memory.</p>
<p><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Blackwood.dll</span> acted as a loader for the open-source Chisel tunneling tool. Once deployed, it enabled the attackers to establish encrypted TCP tunnels over HTTP with SOCKS5 proxy support to bypass perimeter defenses and enable lateral pivoting across compromised networks. To hide the tunneling payload from analysis, the core binary was embedded within the .NET loader as an 8.4 MB manifest resource named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Blackwood.Cheese.xml</span>. This payload was also encrypted with AES-256-CBC.</p>
<p>During execution, the malware derived the decryption key by computing the SHA-256 hash of a hard-coded ASCII passphrase (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">y0Da+QH#pwSg38E?=8R;71-jQu8Tqq</span>). After <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Blackwood.dll</span> decrypted the embedded XML resource, it revealed the actual Chisel payload — a Go-compiled DLL. The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Blackwood.dll</span> loader then reflectively loaded this Chisel DLL into memory and executed it.</p>
<p>The Chisel tool read its operational settings from the external configuration file <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Blackwood.dll.conf</span>, which was dropped alongside the executable. The loader employed a conditional evasion scheme:</p>
<ul>
<li>If the loader binary had a DLL extension, the loader treated the configuration file as Base64-encoded text and decrypted the file via the RC4 algorithm using the hard-coded key “<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">My name is Blackwood !</span>”</li>
<li>If the extension had been changed, the loader would have read the file in plaintext, resulting in a decryption failure.</li>
</ul>
<p>Figure 15 displays the successful decryption using the hard-coded key, yielding a Chisel configuration.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187785" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187785" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187785 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-493507-187630-15.png" alt="Screenshot of a software interface displaying a decryption process. On the left, there's a section for Base64 decoding and RC4 decryption with the key &quot;My name is Blackwood.&quot; The right shows decrypted content from a .conf file, revealing configuration details and client settings. " width="1000" height="667" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-493507-187630-15.png 1634w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-493507-187630-15-660x440.png 660w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-493507-187630-15-1049x700.png 1049w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-493507-187630-15-768x512.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-493507-187630-15-1536x1025.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187785" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 15. A successful decryption of the Blackwood configuration using the hard-coded key.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The discovered IP address, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">91.107.156[.]29</span>, functioned as a dedicated tunneling endpoint. The configuration instructed the infected machine to connect to this server and establish a reverse SOCKS proxy (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">R:0.0.0.0:10999:socks</span>), creating a bridge that could allow attackers to route traffic to the target's internal network.</p>
<h2><a id="post-187630-_7af8blsz5tn"></a>Initial Tool Set Testing</h2>
<p>Throughout the campaign, the attackers performed operational testing to validate and improve their infrastructure and malware functions. The attackers confirmed dead-drop C2 resolution through GitHub comments in November 2025 and simulated Iraqi connections on a mock GitHub issue dashboard in April 2026. We also observed that the attackers tested additional infrastructure on a staging server for a phishing campaign targeting an Israeli entity in May 2026.</p>
<p>A comprehensive analysis of these operational testing phases is provided in Appendix A.</p>
<h2><a id="post-187630-_2hj8a18zn8ed"></a>Additional Credential Harvesting Campaign</h2>
<p>Analysis of Blackwood tunneling configurations submitted to VirusTotal revealed additional attacker infrastructure active between May and June 2026. One of the servers showed that the attackers reused the same infrastructure for both internal network access and credential harvesting. Our research linked this server to a phishing campaign in May–June 2026 targeting an Israeli entity, using conflict-themed lures.</p>
<p>A detailed breakdown of this additional campaign is available in Appendix B.</p>
<h2><a id="post-187630-_gd0aqsy7cbsm"></a>Attribution to the Iranian Nexus</h2>
<p>Despite utilizing cloud infrastructure and code obfuscation to hide their operations, the actors behind the Blinder Tunnel campaign left behind several forensic artifacts. Based on infrastructure ownership, embedded metadata, targeted victimology and overlaps in tradecraft, we assess that an Iranian state-aligned threat actor conducted this campaign.</p>
<p>The key findings that led us to this attribution include:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Iranian-hosted infrastructure</strong>: The initial Blackwood C2 IP address belongs to an Iranian ISP: TOSE'EH ERTEBATAT NOVIN ARIA. A secondary Hetzner tunneling server resolves to Persian-language domains that the attackers likely acquired via an Iranian reseller.</li>
<li><strong>MP3 file metadata</strong>: An <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.mp3</span> file hosted in the attackers' public GitHub repository retained metadata pointing to <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">MusicDel[.]ir</span>, a popular Iranian music platform.</li>
<li><strong>Regional geopolitical victimology</strong>: The campaign's targeting profile aligns with previously documented regional espionage activity and historical targeting patterns associated with this activity cluster.</li>
<li><strong>Convergence with Iranian espionage playbooks</strong>: The campaign employed established Iranian tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), which shows low confidence overlaps between CL-STA-1178 and established Iranian groups. Among the TTPs are:
<ul>
<li>Using aviation-targeted lures</li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">AppDomainManager</span> hijacking to disable ETW (resembling Screening Serpens)</li>
<li>Using GitHub dead-drop resolvers</li>
<li>Using in-memory .NET PowerShell wrappers (resembling <a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/threat-actor-groups-tracked-by-palo-alto-networks-unit-42/#:~:text=Government-,Agent%20Serpens,-Also%20Known%20As" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Serpens</a>)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>A detailed technical breakdown of the attribution artifacts is available in Appendix C.</p>
<h2><a id="post-187630-_2an8ryq91inv"></a>Conclusion</h2>
<p>The activity tracked as CL-STA-1178 represents targeted operations against Middle Eastern enterprise networks in the newly uncovered campaign Blinder Tunnel.</p>
<p>The attackers behind the activity used tailored social engineering techniques to masquerade as Dubai Airports recruiters, using a trojanized Visual Studio coding challenge to target a high-value job seeker based in Iraq.</p>
<p>The campaign is characterized by misuse of built-in developer tools and DLL sideloading. Attackers also used <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">AppDomainManager</span> hijacking to bypass security monitors like ETW. These evasion techniques enabled the attackers to deploy:</p>
<ul>
<li>The primary loader, ShelbyLoader V2</li>
<li>The custom RAT payload, ShelbyC2 V2</li>
<li>The custom Blackwood tunneling tool</li>
</ul>
<p>The Blinder Tunnel campaign relied on living-off-the-cloud techniques. By misusing GitHub APIs and reading encrypted comments within GitHub issues to rotate C2 servers, the attackers disguised the malware’s command traffic as legitimate enterprise platform activity.</p>
<p>We assess with high confidence that this activity cluster aligns with the work of an Iranian-nexus threat actor. The attacker using infrastructure themed around the TV show “Peaky Blinders” links this activity to the campaign previously documented in Elastic Security’s “The Shelby Strategy” report. Furthermore, OpSec failures and flawed cryptography uncovered a parallel campaign targeting an Israeli entity, revealing a broader operational footprint. The campaign's tool set and geographical targeting align with established regional threat activity and historical tradecraft.</p>
<p>This operation underscores the need for organizations to secure developer environments, monitor anomalous cloud platform traffic and maintain vigilance against industry-specific social engineering lures.</p>
