<li><a href="https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/drokbk-malware-uses-github-as-dead-drop-resolver" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Drokbk Malware Uses GitHub as Dead Drop Resolver</a> – Sophos</li>
<li><a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tracking-iran-apt-screening-serpens/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Tracking Iranian APT Screening Serpens’ 2026 Espionage Campaigns</a> – Unit 42</li>
</ul>
<h2><a id="post-187630-_qwp9wrwd8kxp"></a>Appendix A: The Attackers’ Initial Testing of Their Tool Set</h2>
<p>According to our observations, the attackers conducted multiple operational tests throughout the campaign to validate and refine their own tools.</p>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_96rncem6mjzs"></a>First Observed GitHub Comment</h3>
<p>On Nov. 18, 2025, it appears that the threat actor performed operational tests to validate their C2 mechanisms, using a public GitHub repository to test their dead-drop resolution capabilities. By embedding an encrypted payload block inside a comment, the malware developers could verify that their malware located and retrieved fallback C2 instructions.</p>
<p>This early activity suggests a prolonged preparation period, indicating that this campaign could have started in November 2025. Figure 17 shows the comment left by the threat actor.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187818" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187818" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187818 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-502960-187630-18.png" alt="Screenshot of a GitHub edit history shows a comment created by &quot;peakyblinders-tm&quot; on Nov 18, 2025. Two annotations highlight details: one shows the regular expression used to find a specific comment, and the other indicates an encrypted blob containing backup data." width="1000" height="425" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-502960-187630-18.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-502960-187630-18-786x334.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-502960-187630-18-1646x700.png 1646w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-502960-187630-18-768x327.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-502960-187630-18-1536x653.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187818" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 18. A GitHub comment indicating campaign preparation began by November 2025.</figcaption></figure>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_h89vfb4svjej"></a>Analysis of the “asasas” GitHub Thread</h3>
<p>On April 24, 2026, the operators used a GitHub issue in their <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">peakyblinders-tm</span> repository as an operational logging dashboard. The issue's <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">asasas</span> title and an initial <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">hisasas</span> comment suggest that the attackers created this thread as a preliminary trial run. These strings indicate adjacent QWERTY key smashing, typical of a quick confidence check to verify permissions before logging real telemetry.</p>
<p>The thread contained a series of additional comments that appeared to be automated alerts posted by the repository owner. These alerts flagged events such as <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">New device Found</span> and <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Login detected</span>. The thread also contained system attributes such as <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">#microsoft</span> to denote the host operating system.</p>
<p>One of the log entries records a connection from the IP address <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">138<strong>.</strong>256<strong>.</strong>21[.]23</span> alongside the country code for Iraq, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">IQ</span>. Since <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.256</span> exceeds the maximum IPv4 octet value of 255, we assess that attackers used a fabricated, non-routable IP address during an operational test to avoid triggering real network traffic. Despite the invalid IP address, the explicit inclusion of the IQ country code suggests a connection to the campaign's geographic targeting focus in the Middle East.</p>
<p>Figure 18 shows the GitHub issue thread, displaying a sequence of comments from the repository owner that combine what appear to be test strings, mock connection data and automated alerts.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187829" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187829" style="width: 800px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187829 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-507199-187630-19.png" alt="Screenshot of a GitHub issue titled &quot;asasas #1&quot; in the &quot;peakyblinders-tm&quot; repository. The issue is open and contains comments with cautionary messages. One comment notes an IP address and country, while another mentions &quot;Login detected&quot; with a mention of the user." width="800" height="1160" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-507199-187630-19.png 890w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-507199-187630-19-304x440.png 304w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-507199-187630-19-483x700.png 483w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-507199-187630-19-768x1113.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 800px) 100vw, 800px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187829" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 19. GitHub issue “asasas” and comments thread.</figcaption></figure>
<h2><a id="post-187630-_rxhq5vn56uar"></a>Appendix B: Additional Credential Harvesting Campaign</h2>
<p>The server <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">65.109.214[.]145</span> was identified through a Blackwood malware sample submitted to VirusTotal on May 24, 2026. Analysis indicates that this IP address was central to a credential-harvesting campaign between May and June 2026, hosting phishing domains as well as the backend <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Blackwood.dll</span> component, configured on port 8080.</p>
<p>The server hosted a targeted infrastructure consisting of several Google-themed typosquatted domains. These included:</p>
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">cloud.g-drive[.]cam</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">googeldrive[.]cam, drivegoogel[.]cam</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">googelmeet[.]online</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">meetonline[.]cam</span></li>
</ul>
<p>On May 16, 2026, a VirusTotal submitter from Israel submitted a phishing URL hosted on this IP address: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">hxxps[:]//cloud.g-drive[.]cam/drive/file/d/[generated id]/view</span></p>
<p>The underlying landing page was designed to look like a Google Drive error page displaying a prompt to download an archive file named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">WarUnPublishedDocuments.zip</span>.</p>
<p>Clicking the download button shown in Figure 19 directed the target to a site impersonating a Google login portal to collect user credentials at <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">hxxps[:]//cloud.g-drive[.]cam/signin/v2/identifier?from=landing</span>.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187840" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187840" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187840 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-509699-187630-20.png" alt="A dark interface displays a file named &quot;WarUnpublishedDocuments.zip.&quot; A message in the center says, &quot;Couldn't preview file. You may be offline or with limited connectivity. Try downloading instead.&quot; Below the message is a blue &quot;Download&quot; button." width="1000" height="620" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-509699-187630-20.png 1512w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-509699-187630-20-709x440.png 709w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-509699-187630-20-1128x700.png 1128w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-509699-187630-20-768x476.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187840" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 20. A window impersonating Google Drive to lure the target to download a ZIP file named<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;"> WarUnPublishedDocuments.zip</span>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>We reported this information to Google, who investigated the activity outlined in this report. They confirmed that Google Drive systems and infrastructure were not compromised or involved in any way in the attacks.</p>
<p>The threat actors utilized external lookalike domains designed to impersonate Google Drive and Google Workspace interfaces for credential harvesting. Google Safe Browsing and Chrome protections actively block access to these identified malicious domains.</p>
<p>Google noted that they encourage organizations to enforce phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (such as passkeys) and advise users to verify destination URLs before entering account credentials.</p>
<p>Further infrastructure tracking revealed the threat actor’s earlier staging environment. By pivoting on domains hosted on the primary <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">65.109.214[.]145</span> server, we discovered the domain <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">asdfafadafg[.]online</span>. This domain resolved to a secondary IP address, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">38.180.136[.]127</span>.</p>
<p>Timeline analysis indicates that the operators used this server to test their phishing infrastructure during early May 2026, before migrating their operations to the primary <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">65.109.214[.]145</span> server.</p>
<h2><a id="post-187630-_b2fyv8gvfafc"></a>Appendix C: Attribution to the Iranian Nexus</h2>
<p>Despite the attackers’ use of code obfuscation to hide their tracks, we discovered infrastructure overlaps and operational mistakes that revealed key attribution artifacts. An Iranian IP address, embedded music metadata and the targeted activity against critical infrastructure in the Middle East point to an Iranian state-sponsored espionage operation. We summarize each forensic artifact and share how it aligns with our attribution process.</p>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_z1tkqcg4trrf"></a>Infrastructure</h3>
<p>Our investigation into the Blackwood malware samples revealed four IP addresses used in the activity cluster. Two of the identified IP addresses provided clues to the operator’s country of origin.</p>
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">87.248.129[.]239</span><br />
This server was identified through an initial Blackwood malware sample submitted to VirusTotal on May 25, 2025, prior to the current campaign. This is an Iranian IP address, hosted by the internet service provider TOSE'EH ERTEBATAT NOVIN ARIA CO PJS. Active between April and June 2025, this server was the first to be linked to the Blackwood malware.</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">91.107.156[.]29</span><br />
Extracted from the embedded configuration file inside the Blackwood malware sample, the IP address <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">91.107.156[.]29</span> functions as a tunneling relay. Although this server is hosted on Hetzner's infrastructure in Germany, passive DNS telemetry links it to an external domain layout. Historical DNS records reveal subdomains pointing to <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">ns1.soroshpasargad[.]com</span> and to the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">3ff7dfc547e8697c</span> registrar. In Persian, Sorosh means messenger or angel. Pasargad refers to the ancient capital of the first Persian Empire. Based on the aforementioned Persian domain and other Persian domains under the same registrar, we suspect that the current server listed under Hetzner could have been acquired from an Iranian reseller.</li>
</ul>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_ta1x8pvz9r8r"></a>Tool Set</h3>
<p>An OpSec oversight on the attackers' public GitHub profile provided an indicator of the operators' regional origin. The threat actor maintained a public repository under the organization profile <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">peakyblinders-tm</span>. The repository's README file included an embedded audio file titled <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Peaky Blinders Team.mp3</span>, featuring the television show's theme song, “Red Right Hand.”</p>
<p>Figure 20 shows the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Readme.md</span> file from the attacker's public GitHub repository.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187851" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187851" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187851 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-512371-187630-21.png" alt="A GitHub page titled &quot;Peaky Blinders Team&quot; featuring artwork of a person in formal attire with a vintage style. The name &quot;Peaky Blinders Team&quot; is prominently displayed in large text below the image. There's a highlighted section indicating a file name." width="1000" height="897" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-512371-187630-21.png 1204w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-512371-187630-21-491x440.png 491w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-512371-187630-21-780x700.png 780w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-512371-187630-21-768x689.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187851" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 21. The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Readme.md</span> file from the attacker's public GitHub repository features the “Peaky Blinders” theme song.</figcaption></figure>
<p>An analysis of the audio file's embedded metadata revealed that the operators did not strip the file's original attributes before uploading it to their public project page. As shown in the metadata breakdown in Figure 21, the COMMENT field explicitly retains the value <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">MusicDel[.]ir</span>.</p>
<figure id="attachment_187862" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-187862" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-187862 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-516487-187630-22.png" alt="An album audio file information display shows: Artist - Nick Cave &amp; The Bad Seeds; Comment - MusicDel.ir; Title - red right hand; Track - 1." width="1000" height="374" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-516487-187630-22.png 1124w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-516487-187630-22-786x294.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/word-image-516487-187630-22-768x287.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-187862" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 22. Metadata of the audio file.</figcaption></figure>
<p><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">MusicDel[.]ir</span> is an active, public Iranian music distribution website used primarily for downloading tracks in Iran. The presence of this specific metadata string indicates that the operators downloaded the audio file from a domestic Iranian platform before uploading it to their GitHub infrastructure.</p>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_xj6zzzm3bzyx"></a>Victimology</h3>
<p>The targeting profile corresponds with victimology previously observed across other Iranian APT campaigns. The targets were all in the Middle East, specifically within the telecommunications and aviation sectors:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Iraq:</strong> In their research on “<a href="https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/the-shelby-strategy" target="_blank" rel="noopener">The Shelby Strategy</a>,” Elastic Security Labs documented that the threat actor executed spear phishing campaigns from within a compromised Iraqi telecommunications infrastructure. According to their findings, this activity targeted two separate Iraqi communications companies. The activity’s geographic focus was the same in the campaign we investigated. This is corroborated by recent technical artifacts, as multiple campaign-related payloads — including the job assignment archive — were submitted to VirusTotal from Iraq. Additionally, the operators used the country code <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">IQ</span> (Iraq) in their mock connection logs during their GitHub operational testing. Based on the established operational profile and technical evidence linking this activity to the region, we assess that the individual targeted in Blinder Tunnel matches the profile of a software engineer based in Iraq.</li>
<li><strong>United Arab Emirates (UAE):</strong> The initial lure mimicked the Dubai Airports IT Department. In another aviation-themed operation, Elastic Security Labs identified related infrastructure targeting the UAE aviation sector, including the malicious subdomain <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">portal.sharjahairport[.]cloud</span>.</li>
<li><strong>Israel:</strong> The activity also targeted an Israeli entity using conflict-themed social engineering lures. A suspicious URL was submitted to VirusTotal via the web interface from an IP address in Israel. The URL redirected to a phishing page that served an archive named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">WarUnPublishedDocuments.zip</span>, which in turn led to a site impersonating a Google login portal.</li>
</ul>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_4qt5lbe09gw5"></a>The “Peaky Blinders” Theme</h3>
<p>Throughout past and present campaigns (2025-2026), the threat actor behind this activity consistently used a “Peaky Blinders” theme in naming their malware architecture and GitHub-based C2 repositories. This is evident in the following:</p>
<ul>
<li>GitHub accounts named after the show’s name and main characters:
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">peakyblinders-tm</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">ArthurShelby</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">JohnShelllby</span></li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>A repository referencing the gang's clothing: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">GreenBeret0</span></li>
<li>The presence of the show’s theme song in the repo's README file</li>
</ul>
<p>These indicators served as a unique fingerprint that aided in attribution.</p>
<h3><a id="post-187630-_ravkbw7od1nw"></a>Similarities to Other Known APTs</h3>
<p>Public threat intelligence tracks the Blinder Tunnel campaign as disparate activities independent of any known group. Unit 42 tracks this activity as a cluster, specifically using the CL-STA-1178 moniker. The tradecraft used in the Blinder Tunnel campaign shows low-confidence overlaps with established Iranian groups, none of which are strong enough to attribute CL-STA-1178 to any of these groups specifically. However, we do attribute the activity with high confidence to Iranian state-aligned attackers.</p>
<h4><a id="post-187630-_93serx2rmd3l"></a>Screening Serpens</h4>
<p>As detailed in a recent <a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tracking-iran-apt-screening-serpens/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Unit 42 report</a>, the Screening Serpens (aka UNC1549, Smoke Sandstorm, Iranian Dream Job) group targets technology, aerospace and defense professionals in the Middle East using highly tailored social engineering lures. The group has used personalized recruitment offers designed to trick targets into initiating the infection chain.</p>
<p>Another evolution highlighted in our research is the use of .NET <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">AppDomainManager</span> hijacking, manipulating legitimate configuration files to disable endpoint security mechanisms before the malware executes.</p>
<p>The Blinder Tunnel campaign employs both tactics. The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Dubai Airport Coding</span> Challenge deployment aligns with Screening Serpens' pattern of fraudulent hiring lures targeting the aviation sector.</p>
<p>Manipulation of the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RuntimeBroker.exe.config</span> file to execute <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">AppDomainManager</span> hijacking, to disable ETW (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">&lt;etwEnable enabled="false"/&gt;</span>), was used by Screening Serpens throughout 2026.</p>
<h4><a id="post-187630-_atvbd8zccavv"></a>Agent Serpens</h4>
<p>When analyzing the Iranian state-sponsored activity tracked as <a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/threat-actor-groups-tracked-by-palo-alto-networks-unit-42/#:~:text=Government-,Agent%20Serpens,-Also%20Known%20As" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Serpens</a> (aka APT35, Charming Kitten, Phosphorus), we noticed additional similarities in its operational playbook.</p>
<p>An overlap between this Blinder Tunnel campaign and Agent Serpens activity is the misuse of trusted developer platforms to maintain resilient C2 infrastructure. If communication channels fail, both campaigns rely on GitHub as a fallback dead-drop resolver.</p>
<p>As described in this research, the ShelbyLoader V2 backdoor queries the GitHub Issues Search API to extract AES-encrypted routing data hidden within HTML comments. Similarly, <a href="https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/drokbk-malware-uses-github-as-dead-drop-resolver" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Drokbk malware</a> uses the GitHub API to parse a specific repository file to locate and re-establish its C2 connection.</p>
<p>Furthermore, <a href="https://www.cybereason.com/blog/research/powerless-trojan-iranian-apt-phosphorus-adds-new-powershell-backdoor-for-espionage" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cybereason's analysis</a> of the Iranian threat group highlights a similar PowerShell execution technique. Just as Blinder Tunnel operations rely on memory-only wrappers, Agent Serpens deploys the PowerLess Trojan to execute PowerShell commands within a native .NET context. In both cases, the techniques used prevented the creation of a suspicious <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">PowerShell.exe</span> process that could trigger event detection alerts.</p>

<script>
 var PAN_LOAD_RECAPTCHA_LANGUAGE = 'en_US';

(function($) {
	// Migrated from the unit42-v5 + Modifications
	var subscribeSuccess = false;
	var email = document.getElementById('newsletter-email');
	var subscription_form = document.getElementById('unit42footerSubscription_form');
	var subscription_form_button = document.getElementById('unit42footerSubscription_form_button');
        var isCaptchaComplete02  = false;	
        window.captchaInlineFormOnload = function(token){
            isCaptchaComplete02 = true;
            $("form[name='Unit42_Subscribe'] button[id='unit42footerSubscription_form_button']").prop('disabled', false);
        }
        var PAN_INLINE_FORM_RECAPTCHA_LOADED = false;
        const SITE_KEY = '6LdDKhIsAAAAABdoYV3PR5VJ2Gz23_dLSvq2uvBQ'; 
                if(!PAN_INLINE_FORM_RECAPTCHA_LOADED){
               PAN_INLINE_FORM_RECAPTCHA_LOADED = true;
               // trigger loading api.js (recaptcha.js) script
               var recapthaScript = $("script[src='https://www.google.com/recaptcha/enterprise.js?render="+SITE_KEY+"&hl="+PAN_LOAD_RECAPTCHA_LANGUAGE+"&onload=captchaInlineFormOnload']").length
               // console.log("recapthaScript",recapthaScript);
               if (!recapthaScript) {
                   var head = document.getElementsByTagName('head')[0];
                   var script = document.createElement('script');
                   script.typerecapthaScript = 'text/javascript';
                   script.src = "https://www.google.com/recaptcha/enterprise.js?render="+SITE_KEY+"&hl="+PAN_LOAD_RECAPTCHA_LANGUAGE+"&onload=captchaInlineFormOnload";
                   head.appendChild(script);
               }
               else{
                   captchaInlineFormOnload();
                }
           }
            	
	
	$(subscription_form).submit(function(e) {
		e.preventDefault();
		e.stopImmediatePropagation();
		updateEmailMask();
		var success = true;
		var form = $(this);
		var mail = form.find('input[name="Email"]');
		
		if (mail.val() === '') {
			mail.addClass('has-error');
			showError(1);
			success = false;	
		}  else if (!isEmail(mail.val())){
			showError(2);
			success = false;
		}
		else {
			mail.removeClass('has-error');
			$('.error-mail').addClass('d-none');
		}

		

		if (success) {
                                                if(grecaptcha){
                        grecaptcha.enterprise.ready(function() {
                            grecaptcha.enterprise.execute(SITE_KEY, {action: 'submit'}).then(function(token) {
                                submitSubscribeForm({token :token, action : 'submit'},form);
                            });
                        });
                    }
                    			
		}
		return false;
	});
        function submitSubscribeForm(tokenData, form){
            var serialized_data = form.serialize();
            let captchaParams = `&g-recaptcha-response=${tokenData.token}&action=${tokenData.action}`;
            $.ajax({
				type: 'POST',
				url: form.attr('action'),
				data: serialized_data+captchaParams,
				beforeSend: function() {
                 form.find('button').addClass('is-loading');
    			},
				success: function(msg) {
					form.find('.form-success-message').html('<p class="success-message">You have been successfully subscribed</p>');
					form.find('button').removeClass('is-loading');
					$(email).val('');
					clearError();
				},
				error: function(jqXHR, textStatus, errorThrown) {
					$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled', true);
					form.find('button').removeClass('is-loading');
					
				}
			});
            
        }
	function showError(error_type){
		if(error_type == 1) {
			$('.error-mail').text("Please enter the email address.").addClass('error-show');
			$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled');
		} else if(error_type == 2){
			$('.error-mail').text("Please provide a valid e-mail address.").addClass('error-show');
			$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled');
		}	
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-loading');
	}
	function clearError(){
		$('.error-mail').text("").removeClass('error-show');;
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-loading');
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-disabled');
	}
	
	$(email).on('input', function (event) { 
		var email = $(this).val();
		if (isEmail(email) ) {			
			clearError();
		} else if(email == ""){
			clearError();
		} else{
			showError(2);			  
		}
    });

	function isEmail(email) {
		var re = /^(([^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+(\.[^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+)*)|(".+"))@((\[[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\])|(([a-zA-Z\-0-9]+\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,}))$/;
		return re.test(String(email).toLowerCase());
	}
	
	
	
	function updateEmailMask() {
		var email = $("#unit42footerSubscription_form input[name='Email']").val();
		if (email && email.trim() != '') {
			var maskedEmail = maskEmailAddress(email);
			$("#unit42footerSubscription_form input[name='emailFormMask']").val(maskedEmail);
		}
	}

	function maskEmailAddress (emailAddress) {
		function mask(str) {
			var strLen = str.length;
			if (strLen > 4) {
				return str.substr(0, 1) + str.substr(1, strLen - 1).replace(/\w/g, '*') + str.substr(-1,1);
			}
			return str.replace(/\w/g, '*');
		}
		return emailAddress.replace(/([\w.]+)@([\w.]+)(\.[\w.]+)/g, function (m, p1, p2, p3) {
			return mask(p1) + '@' + mask(p2) + p3;
		});

		return emailAddress;
	}

}(jQuery));
//# sourceMappingURL=main.js.map
	
</script>

<script type="text/javascript">
	$(document).ready(function(){
		$("html").on("click", ".language-btn", function () {
			$(this).toggleClass("expand");
			$(".language-dropdown").toggleClass("expand");
		});

		$("html").on("click", "body", function (b) {
			if (!$(b.target).is(".language-btn")) {
				$(".language-btn").removeClass("expand");
				$(".language-dropdown").removeClass("expand");
			}
		});
	});
</script>

	var isProcessing = false; 
    function alter_ul_post_values(obj,post_id,ul_type){
	
		if (isProcessing)    
		return;  
		isProcessing = true;   
		var like_nonce = jQuery('#_wpnonce').val();
		jQuery(obj).find("span").html("..");
                jQuery.ajax({
                    type: "POST",
                    url: "https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/plugins/like-dislike-counter-for-posts-pages-and-comments/ajax_counter.php",
                    data: "post_id="+post_id+"&up_type="+ul_type+"&ul_nonce="+like_nonce,
                    success: function(msg){
                            jQuery(obj).find("span").html(msg);
                            isProcessing = false; 
                            jQuery(obj).find('svg').children('path').attr('stroke','#0050FF');
                            jQuery(obj).removeClass('idc_ul_cont_not_liked idc_ul_cont_not_liked_inner');
                    }
 		});
	}

function loadScript(url, defer){
    var script1 = document.createElement('script');
    script1.setAttribute('type', 'text/javascript');
    script1.setAttribute('src',url);
    if(defer == true){
        script1.setAttribute('defer','defer');
    }
    document.head.appendChild(script1);
}
function loadScript1(url, callback){

    var script = document.createElement("script")
    script.type = "text/javascript";
    if (script.readyState){  //IE
        script.onreadystatechange = function(){
            if (script.readyState == "loaded" || script.readyState == "complete"){
                script.onreadystatechange = null;
                callback();
            }
        };
    } else {  //Others
        script.onload = function(){
            callback();
        };
    }
    script.src = url;
    document.getElementsByTagName("head")[0].appendChild(script);
}

    setTimeout(function(){

          }, 3000);

document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function() {
  // Find all the forms on the page
  var forms = document.getElementsByTagName("form");

  // Loop through each form
  for (var i = 0; i < forms.length; i++) {
    var form = forms[i];

    // Check if the hidden input field already exists
    var requestInput = form.querySelector("input[name='web_unit42_req_id']");
    if (!requestInput) {
      // Create a hidden input element if it doesn't exist
      requestInput = document.createElement("input");
      requestInput.type = "hidden";
      requestInput.name = "web_unit42_req_id";
      requestInput.id = "web_unit42_req_id";

      // Append the hidden field to the form
      form.appendChild(requestInput);
    }
  }
});

// Assign the onCheqResponse function to the window object to handle events from any form
window.onCheqResponse = function(encryptedMessage, requestID) {
  // Find all the forms on the page
  var forms = document.getElementsByTagName("form");

  for (var i = 0; i < forms.length; i++) {
    var form = forms[i];
    var requestInput = form.querySelector("input[name='web_unit42_req_id']");
    if (requestInput) {
      requestInput.value = requestID;
    }
  }
};
